questions.title: Shell variation across a town
questions.stem:
The photographs show examples of colour and banding. In a new survey, researchers counted yellow and non-yellow adult snails at 12 urban and 12 woodland sites. Each site contributed 20 snails. Temperatures represent mean afternoon ground temperature. The counts are pooled across sites.

| Habitat | Yellow | Non-yellow | Mean ground temperature / °C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Urban | 150 | 90 | 28.4 |
| Woodland | 96 | 144 | 23.1 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage of yellow snails in each habitat and express the difference in percentage points.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish a colour category from a banding category using the photographs. Why would recording colour alone lose information?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Propose a selection mechanism that could produce the urban pattern. State a necessary condition for a response across generations.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Why would treating all 240 snails in one habitat as independent temperature replicates exaggerate the evidence? Propose a site-level analysis.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Design a comparison that tests a thermal effect of colour while controlling a plausible confounder.

steps.text: Difference is 22.5 percentage points (urban higher).
Pink and yellow describe background colour whereas banding describes presence or number of dark bands.
The two pink shells shown have different banding patterns, so pooling them hides variation.
Under equivalent exposure, a paler shell could absorb less radiation, reducing heat stress; accept a supported alternative involving predators.
If surviving individuals leave more offspring, the colour-associated variants may increase in frequency.
Differences in shell colour must have a heritable component.
Snails within one site experience shared conditions and are nested within that site.
Calculate each site's yellow proportion and compare it with that site's temperature across the independent sites.
Expose comparable shells or live snails of different colours to standardized light and measure temperature change over the same interval.
Match or randomize banding, size, orientation or substrate; repeat for multiple independent specimens.

questions.title: Carbon uptake and cell respiration
questions.stem: An algal suspension in light produces a net 2.4 mg O₂ h⁻¹. In darkness the same amount of algae consumes 0.6 mg O₂ h⁻¹. Assume comparable conditions and a constant respiration rate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate gross oxygen production in light. Explain the need for the dark measurement.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the chloroplast and mitochondrion contribute to carbon cycling within these cells.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give a reason the dark correction could be biased and a control for an abiotic change in measured oxygen.

steps.text: Gross rate=2.4+0.6=3.0 mg O₂ h⁻¹.
In light, photosynthesis produces oxygen while respiration consumes some simultaneously.
The dark measurement estimates consumption when photosynthetic production is absent.
Photosynthesis incorporates inorganic CO₂ into organic compounds using light energy.
Respiration breaks down organic substrates, releasing CO₂.
The carbon released can become available for photosynthesis again.
Respiration in darkness may differ from respiration in light, or temperature may change during measurement.
Run the same illuminated and dark solutions without algae to estimate sensor drift or physical gas exchange.

questions.title: Transport from lung to artery
questions.stem: At rest, a student's stroke volume is 68 cm³ beat⁻¹ and heart rate is 72 beats min⁻¹. During steady exercise these increase to 95 cm³ beat⁻¹ and 132 beats min⁻¹. Use cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. In a simplified tracer study, the first detections after a pulse at the lung capillaries were: left ventricle, 2.2 s; aorta, 2.7 s; pulmonary vein, 0.8 s; left atrium, 1.4 s. The mitral valve connects the two left chambers and the aortic valve connects the ventricle to the aorta.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate cardiac output in dm³ min⁻¹ for both conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the detection times to reconstruct the tracer's route from the lung capillaries to the aorta. Identify where each of the two valves is crossed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why elevated cardiac output alone cannot establish that muscle oxygen consumption rose by the same factor.

steps.text: Exercise=95×132/1000=12.54 dm³ min⁻¹.
Pulmonary veins carry the oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
It passes through the left atrioventricular (mitral) valve to the left ventricle.
It leaves through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta.
Consumption also depends on the difference in oxygen content between arterial and venous blood.
The fraction of total blood flow reaching active muscles can change.

questions.title: From coding sequence to phenotype
questions.stem: A coding strand segment changes from 5′-GCT TTT GAA-3′ to 5′-GCT TTC GAA-3′. Use the mRNA codon assignments GCU=Ala, UUU=Phe, UUC=Phe and GAA=Glu.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Give the original mRNA sequence and amino acid sequence with direction of reading indicated.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the mutation type at the nucleotide level and its effect on the polypeptide segment.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the likely consequence of deleting the first T of the original TTT triplet. Explain why DNA sequence alone cannot establish the size of a phenotypic effect.

steps.text: 5′-GCU UUU GAA-3′, read 5′ to 3′.
Ala–Phe–Glu.
It is a single-base substitution (T→C in the coding strand).
The change is synonymous since UUC and UUU both encode phenylalanine, so this segment's amino acid sequence is unchanged.
A one-base deletion shifts the grouping of downstream codons.
It can alter downstream amino acids or introduce an early stop.
Phenotypic outcome also depends on protein function, position, expression or compensation by another allele.

questions.title: Keeping pathogens out and remembering infection
questions.stem: A respiratory pathogen enters through mucosal surfaces. Some previously exposed individuals develop a faster specific response on re-exposure.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline three ways barriers reduce entry or establishment of pathogens.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a phagocyte helps contain microbes that have crossed a barrier.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain a specific antibody response to an antigen and why re-exposure can produce a faster response.

parts.label: quality
parts.prompt: Quality of the complete extended response

steps.text: Mucus traps particles and microorganisms.
Cilia move trapped material toward removal from the airway.
Intact epithelium forms a physical barrier; accept a suitable additional mucosal or chemical defence.
It recognizes or attaches to a microbe.
It surrounds the microbe with its membrane.
A vesicle containing the microbe forms by engulfment.
It fuses with a lysosome or receives hydrolytic enzymes.
The microbe is digested or destroyed within the cell.
A particular antigen is recognized by a lymphocyte with complementary specificity.
Activation selects specific clones, with helper T-cell signals where appropriate.
Selected B cells divide by mitosis, expanding the clone.
Some differentiate into plasma cells.
Plasma cells secrete antibodies specific to the antigen.
Binding can neutralize the pathogen or facilitate its removal.
Some cells remain as memory cells and rapidly generate a larger response on re-exposure.

Award one mark when the complete response communicates the relevant biological reasoning clearly and concisely, with logical connections and little repetition. Assess this across the parts, independently of the content score.

questions.title: A woodland after a storm
questions.stem: A storm opens a gap in a woodland canopy and leaves fallen branches. Consider both living organisms and dead organic matter.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline how three different feeding roles obtain organic matter in the woodland.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why energy available to a secondary consumer is less than the chemical energy originally captured by producers.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discuss how carbon moves between the atmosphere, fallen wood, decomposers and regrowing trees over time.

parts.label: quality
parts.prompt: Quality of the complete extended response

steps.text: Producers fix inorganic carbon to make organic compounds.
Consumers ingest other organisms or material derived from them.
Saprotrophs digest dead organic material externally and absorb soluble products.
Some producer biomass is never ingested by primary consumers.
Some ingested material is not assimilated and leaves as faeces.
Respiration transfers usable energy from organic compounds and dissipates heat.
Respiratory and other losses also occur at the next trophic transfer.
Only the fraction retained as new biomass is available for a subsequent consumer to incorporate.
Atmospheric CO₂ diffuses into leaves.
Photosynthesis incorporates its carbon into organic compounds.
Trees use some assimilated carbon to make structural biomass such as cellulose.
Fallen wood retains previously fixed carbon after the tree dies.
Decomposer enzymes break down wood and some carbon enters decomposer biomass.
Decomposer and tree respiration return carbon to the atmosphere as CO₂.
Net storage depends on the balance between fixation and release over the period, so regrowth alone does not prove a net sink.

Award one mark when the complete response communicates the relevant biological reasoning clearly and concisely, with logical connections and little repetition. Assess this across the parts, independently of the content score.
